Box Volume

AlgebraAreaLimits
Game: Cut the same little square from each corner of a flat sheet and fold up the sides to make a box.
How to play: Slide the sliders to change the sheet and the cut. Watch the graph: the high point is the cut that makes the biggest box.
11.0
8.5
1.00
Look for the math

A bigger cut makes the walls taller but leaves a smaller base. Somewhere between no cut at all and cutting away half the sheet, the box is as big as it can be. The graph and a little calculus tell us exactly where.

The volume is a cubic

Call the sheet's sides a and b, and the cut x. After the cuts the base is (a − 2x) by (b − 2x) and the height is x, so the volume is

v(x) = x(a − 2x)(b − 2x) = 4x³ − 2(a + b)x² + abx

That is a cubic polynomial with a positive leading coefficient 4 and roots at 0, a/2 and b/2. Those last two roots are where the base shrinks to nothing, so only 0 ≤ x ≤ min(a/2, b/2) makes a real box. The logic test checks the expansion and all three roots for every pair of slider sizes.

Where the graph turns

To find the high point, set the derivative to zero:

v'(x) = 12x² − 4(a + b)x + ab = 0

This quadratic has two roots. The bigger one is the low dip of the graph; the smaller one is the peak we want. Using the minus sign in the formula gives

x = ((a + b) − √(a² − ab + b²)) / 6

The logic test checks this against a fine sweep of every possible cut and confirms it is always the largest volume, and that the cut always lies strictly between 0 and min(a/2, b/2).

A square sheet

When a = b, the two positive roots merge into one double root at a/2: the graph just touches the axis there instead of crossing it. The formula then becomes x = a/6 and the largest box has volume 2a³/27. Try setting both sliders to the same value and pressing Find the best cut — the green dot moves to one sixth of the side.

Exact and approximate answers

The original page uses a = 11, b = 8.5 and notes that dragging in the applet reaches about x = 1.60, while the true answer is the irrational number 1.5854…. The slider and the button here can show only two decimals, so they give an approximation too — but the green dot is placed at the exact value. As Bogomolny points out, an approximation is not the same as an exact solution, and for a real sheet of card it is often all we need.

Keep the sheet fixed and slide only the cut. Does the graph's high point move when you make the sheet longer?
